ripple_effect.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships

historical_precedents.what_happened: On 26 July 2023, General Abdourahamane Tchiani led the presidential guard in removing President Mohamed Bazoum and installed a military council. The regional bloc ECOWAS responded with an ultimatum, then sanctions including closed land and air borders, a no-fly zone on commercial flights, suspension of financial transactions, and asset freezes; Nigeria cut electricity supply to Niger on 2 August 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The West African regional central bank cancelled a planned 30 billion CFA franc (about $51 million) bond issuance for Niger, and the World Bank suspended disbursements to the country. Niger is a significant global uranium exporter, and the coup raised questions over the operations of French nuclear fuel company Orano's mining activities there.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected officials. ripple_effect.name: US territory / sub-sovereign debt restructuring crisis

historical_precedents.event: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring
historical_precedents.what_happened: Puerto Rico's bonds were downgraded to junk status in February 2014, and Governor García Padilla declared the roughly $74 billion in bond debt (plus $49 billion in unfunded pension liabilities) 'not payable' on June 28, 2015; after Puerto Rico missed a $422 million payment on May 1, 2016, Congress passed PROMESA, which President Obama signed June 30, 2016, creating a federal oversight board with authority over the territory's budget and debt restructuring.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022.

possibility_chains: A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

Heavy institutional exposure to a single distressed municipal issuer (in this case, via tax-exempt bond funds that concentrated Puerto Rico debt for its tax advantages) has historically transmitted a regional fiscal crisis into national investment portfolios far from the issuer itself.

Debt-crisis austerity measures layered on top of a shrinking population and tax base have historically been self-reinforcing, since tax increases and service cuts have tended to accelerate the outward migration that shrank the tax base in the first place.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring (2014–2022): Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022. A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

ripple_effect.name: Post-9/11 aviation security overhaul creates the TSA

historical_precedents.event: Aviation and Transportation Security Act signed into law
historical_precedents.what_happened: In response to the September 11, 2001 attacks, US President George W. Bush signed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, creating the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and federalizing airport passenger and baggage screening, which had previously been contracted out by individual airlines to a patchwork of private security companies. The TSA assumed screening responsibility at more than 450 US airports; from February to December 2002 alone, 1.7 million applicants were assessed to fill about 55,000 new federal screening jobs.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The legislation replaced airline-contracted private screening with a single federal agency on a permanent basis; as of fiscal year 2025 the TSA operates on an annual budget of $11.8 billion and employs more than 58,600 people, reflecting the scale of the ongoing security infrastructure the 2001 law created.

possibility_chains: A single catastrophic security failure in commercial aviation has historically triggered a permanent, government-funded expansion of the aviation security regime rather than a temporary response, with the resulting cost structure and screening requirements persisting for decades.

New aviation security requirements imposed after a major incident have historically added recurring cost and passenger friction across the entire air-travel industry, not just the routes or airports directly involved in the triggering incident.

ripple_effect.name: West Germany's Gastarbeiter guest-worker program

historical_precedents.event: West Germany recruits foreign 'guest workers' during its postwar boom
historical_precedents.what_happened: West Germany signed bilateral labor-recruitment agreements with Italy (November 1955), Spain and Greece (March 1960), Turkey (October 1961), Morocco (June 1963), South Korea (December 1963), Portugal (March 1964), Tunisia (October 1965), and Yugoslavia (October 1968) to recruit temporary 'guest workers' (Gastarbeiter) to fill labor shortages during West Germany's postwar economic expansion.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By the 1970s, roughly 2.5 million foreign workers were employed in West Germany, providing labor that supported the country's continued industrial expansion through its 'Wirtschaftswunder' (economic miracle) era.

historical_precedents.event: Turkish recruitment becomes the program's largest single source
historical_precedents.what_happened: Under the October 1961 recruitment agreement with Turkey — modified in 1964 to permit longer stays — about 2.7 million Turkish citizens applied for work in Germany, of whom roughly 750,000 were accepted before recruitment was halted in 1973.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Although the program was designed around temporary worker rotation, many workers remained permanently after recruitment ended; by 2010, roughly 4 million people of Turkish descent lived in Germany, reshaping the country's demographic and labor-market composition for decades after the recruitment program itself ended.

historical_precedents.event: Economic research on the program's native-wage effects
historical_precedents.what_happened: Retrospective economic research examined the wage effects of the Gastarbeiter program's large-scale labor immigration on native West German workers' lifetime earnings.
historical_precedents.market_impact: One widely cited study estimated the program reduced expected discounted lifetime labor income for native West German workers by an average of about 1.51%, with declines reaching as much as 5.91% for the most affected worker groups — a finding subsequently cited in broader debates about the wage effects of large-scale guest-worker immigration programs.

possibility_chains: Guest-worker programs designed around the assumption of temporary rotation have historically underestimated the share of workers who settle permanently, a mismatch that has repeatedly required receiving countries to retroactively build integration, language, and citizenship policy for populations originally treated as transient.

Large recruited-labor inflows concentrated in specific industrial sectors have historically depressed wage growth for native workers most directly competing in those sectors, while more broadly supporting aggregate industrial output and economic growth in the receiving economy.

Second- and third-generation descendants of guest-worker cohorts have historically shown different (often improving, but not fully converged) labor-market and educational outcomes relative to the native-born population, a pattern documented in Germany's Turkish-German population and used as a reference case in later European integration-policy debates.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Economic research on the program's native-wage effects (1955–1973 (retrospective analysis)): One widely cited study estimated the program reduced expected discounted lifetime labor income for native West German workers by an average of about 1.51%, with declines reaching as much as 5.91% for the most affected worker groups — a finding subsequently cited in broader debates about the wage effects of large-scale guest-worker immigration programs. Guest-worker programs designed around the assumption of temporary rotation have historically underestimated the share of workers who settle permanently, a mismatch that has repeatedly required receiving countries to retroactively build integration, language, and citizenship policy for populations originally treated as transient.

linked_playbooks.name: Europe's 2015 migration crisis and labor-market integration
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: High per-capita arrivals in Sweden and Austria (2015): The scale of per-capita arrivals in these smaller economies drove both countries to tighten border and asylum policy in subsequent years, and became a significant driver of domestic political debate across the EU through the following decade. Large, concentrated refugee inflows have historically taken several years — not months — to show up in receiving-country labor-force participation data, since language acquisition, credential recognition, and asylum-processing timelines all impose lags before large-scale employment becomes possible.

linked_playbooks.name: Skilled-worker visa policy shift
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: $100,000 H-1B application fee (19 September 2025 – ongoing): A federal judge ruled the $100,000 fee unlawful on June 8, 2026, but the year-plus of uncertainty in between affected employer hiring and budget planning for new skilled-visa hires, particularly in technology and healthcare roles that rely heavily on the H-1B category. A sudden increase in the cost or difficulty of hiring skilled foreign workers has historically pushed some employers to shift new hiring or entire teams to countries with more accessible immigration systems, a process that has typically played out over a year or more rather than immediately.

historical_precedents.event: Global burden-of-disease estimate for bacterial antimicrobial resistance
historical_precedents.what_happened: A global analysis found bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was directly responsible for an estimated 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 and was associated with roughly 4.95 million deaths that year overall, with Sub-Saharan Africa (23.7 per 100,000) and South Asia (21.5 per 100,000) recording the highest death rates.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The World Bank projected that, left unaddressed, AMR could raise global healthcare costs by roughly $1 trillion and cause annual global economic losses of $1–3.4 trillion by 2030, while the WHO has cited projections warning of up to 10 million deaths a year globally by 2050 without intervention.

historical_precedents.event: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) EU/EEA burden estimate
historical_precedents.what_happened: ECDC documented 671,689 infections in the EU and European Economic Area caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria in 2015.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Those infections were estimated to have caused 33,110 deaths that year — a toll comparable to the combined burden of several other major infectious diseases in the EU — and contributed to sustained EU-level policy pushes for new antibiotic development incentives given weak commercial returns on new antibiotics held in reserve rather than sold at volume.

Around 200-300 people were killed or went missing, including 140 workers at the Tapovan Vishnugad hydropower plant. The flood washed away the Dhauliganga Dam, destroyed the 13-megawatt Rishiganga hydropower project, and destroyed a bridge connecting 13 villages.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Losses to the Tapovan Vishnugad Hydropower Plant alone were estimated at roughly Rs 1,500 crore (about $206 million), illustrating the concentrated financial exposure of hydropower infrastructure built directly in glacier-fed, seismically active mountain river valleys.

possibility_chains: Hydropower and dam infrastructure built in glacier-fed mountain valleys has historically faced a distinct catastrophic-failure risk from sudden glacier or rock-ice collapse, separate from and less predictable than ordinary flood-season risk.

A glacial lake outburst flood or ice avalanche destroying hydropower infrastructure has historically prompted downstream review of dam-siting and early-warning systems across the wider river basin, not just at the directly affected site.

As mountain glaciers continue to retreat, the number of unstable glacial lakes and hanging ice masses above populated valleys and infrastructure has been assessed by glaciologists as growing, though the timing and location of any specific future collapse remains inherently difficult to forecast.

ripple_effect.name: Major corporate data breach and regulatory fallout

historical_precedents.what_happened: Hackers exploited an unpatched web-application vulnerability at credit-reporting agency Equifax between May and July 2017; the company did not publicly disclose the intrusion until September 7, 2017, by which point the personal data - including Social Security numbers - of 147.9 million Americans, 15.2 million UK residents, and roughly 19,000 Canadians had been exposed.
historical_precedents.market_impact: In July 2019, Equifax agreed to a settlement of at least $575 million (potentially rising to $700 million) with the FTC, the CFPB, and 48 U.S. states, including a $300 million victim-compensation fund and $100 million in CFPB penalties; the UK's Financial Conduct Authority separately fined Equifax roughly £11.16 million.

historical_precedents.event: British Airways data breach and ICO fine
historical_precedents.what_happened: Attackers accessed British Airways' website and app between June 22 and September 5, 2018, exposing personal data on roughly 429,000 customers, including payment-card details for about 244,000 of them.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The UK Information Commissioner's Office initially proposed a fine of £183.39 million in 2019 under GDPR, then reduced it to £20 million in its final ruling on October 16, 2020 after accounting for mitigating factors including remediation steps and pandemic-related financial hardship - illustrating both the scale GDPR penalties can reach and how much regulators can discount them in practice.

possibility_chains: A large consumer data breach has historically triggered a multi-year regulatory and litigation process whose final financial penalty often lands well below initial headline estimates.
Breaches involving financial or credit data have historically prompted broader legislative and regulatory scrutiny of the entire sector the breached company operates in, not just the company itself.
Companies that suffer high-profile breaches have historically faced elevated compliance and cybersecurity insurance costs for years afterward, independent of the direct settlement costs.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: British Airways data breach and ICO fine (June - September 2018 (fine issued October 2020)): The UK Information Commissioner's Office initially proposed a fine of £183.39 million in 2019 under GDPR, then reduced it to £20 million in its final ruling on October 16, 2020 after accounting for mitigating factors including remediation steps and pandemic-related financial hardship - illustrating both the scale GDPR penalties can reach and how much regulators can discount them in practice. A large consumer data breach has historically triggered a multi-year regulatory and litigation process whose final financial penalty often lands well below initial headline estimates.

linked_playbooks.name: Fintech / payments company collapse from accounting fraud
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Wirecard collapse, Germany (June–August 2020): Wirecard's stock fell 72% over two trading days and the company was removed from Germany's DAX index; German prosecutors opened criminal investigations and the German parliament launched an inquiry into regulatory failures by BaFin, the financial regulator that had repeatedly defended Wirecard against the fraud allegations. A fintech or payments company built on rapid growth and thin regulatory oversight has historically been vulnerable to accounting fraud going undetected for years, since fast-growing complex international operations can be harder for regulators and auditors to fully verify.

linked_playbooks.name: Major cryptocurrency regulatory shift or exchange collapse
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Collapse of the FTX cryptocurrency exchange (November 2022): FTX was found to owe as much as $8 billion, prompting SEC and CFTC investigations and federal charges against Bankman-Fried in December 2022; a bankruptcy court later ordered FTX's estate to pay $12.7 billion in compensation to former customers in August 2024. A major national ban or crackdown on cryptocurrency activity has historically caused an immediate drop in crypto prices, followed by a longer-run relocation of affected activity (such as mining) to jurisdictions with friendlier rules.

linked_playbooks.name: Cyberattack on critical infrastructure
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: NotPetya malware outbreak (June 2017): Maersk had to reinstall its entire global IT infrastructure and briefly ran port terminal operations manually; total global damages were later estimated at over $10 billion, making it one of the most costly cyberattacks in history. A cyberattack that forces critical infrastructure offline (pipelines, ports, power grids) has historically caused localized shortages and price spikes in the directly affected region, even when the underlying supply elsewhere is unaffected.

ripple_effect.name: South China Sea territorial and shipping dispute

historical_precedents.event: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Philippines brought a case to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in January 2013 challenging China's expansive 'nine-dash line' claim over most of the South China Sea. The tribunal ruled on 12 July 2016 that China's historic-rights claim had no lawful basis under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that none of the disputed Spratly Islands features qualified as islands generating their own exclusive economic zone.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits.

possibility_chains: Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

Legal rulings against a claimant state in international tribunals have historically been rejected by the losing party when core territorial claims are involved, meaning such rulings have tended to shape diplomatic and legal leverage over years rather than immediately resolve the dispute.

Long-running territorial disputes in contested waters have historically constrained joint oil and gas exploration in the same areas, since companies are typically reluctant to invest amid unresolved sovereignty claims.

The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits. Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

linked_playbooks.name: Critical shipping route disruption
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea (Late 2023 – ongoing): Many major shipping lines rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding roughly 10–14 days to typical Asia–Europe voyages and pushing container freight rates sharply higher on affected routes. Disruption to a major shipping chokepoint has historically forced vessels onto longer alternate routes, raising fuel and time costs that carriers have often passed on as higher freight rates.

linked_playbooks.name: International court ruling on a territorial or trade dispute
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Philippines v. China South China Sea arbitration (2013–2016): China rejected the ruling outright and continued its activities in the disputed waters, showing that, unlike the Bakassi case where the losing party ultimately complied, an international ruling does not automatically compel compliance from a major power that rejects the tribunal's jurisdiction. International court rulings on territorial or maritime disputes have historically been complied with when the losing government has a political and diplomatic interest in maintaining its standing with the court system, as in the Bakassi case, but have been rejected outright by major powers unwilling to accept binding third-party jurisdiction over sovereignty claims, as in the South China Sea case.

linked_playbooks.name: Taiwan Strait military and political tension
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's military exercises following U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan (August 2022): Airlines and shipping operators rerouted some flights and vessels around the announced exercise and exclusion zones surrounding Taiwan for the duration of the drills. Periods of heightened Taiwan Strait tension have historically prompted temporary rerouting of commercial shipping and air traffic around announced exercise or exclusion zones, given Taiwan's location on major East Asia air and sea routes.
